scenario: A vendor tracker outgrew its spreadsheet. A teammate sends a feature comparison chart and wants to pick a tool today.
question: What do you do before looking at tools?

options.text: Describe the work on one page: the records, links, volume, people, rhythm and triggers.
Pick the tool with the most features listed on the chart.
Pick whichever tool the team already uses for notes.

why: Most bad tool choices happen because the comparison started with the tool. Familiarity is worth something, but it is not the same as fit.

scenario: Your team writes lots of runbooks and meeting notes, and each record needs a written explanation alongside its data.
question: Which tool's center of gravity fits best?

options.text: Notion: a workspace where documents and databases live together, with each record able to open as a full page.
Smartsheet, because it is a grid.
None. A single shared document will do.

why: Each product's design follows from what it was built around. Notion's center is the page, which suits work where explanation and data sit side by side.

scenario: You need to share a vendor view with an outside contractor, but the table also holds sensitive contract terms.
question: What do you check in the trial?

options.text: Whether access can be limited to some records or fields, whether a view can be shared without exposing the rest, how seats are counted, whether an audit log exists and which plan includes it.
Nothing yet. The marketing page says it is secure.
Share the whole table and tell the contractor to ignore the other rows.

why: Permissions are where the tools differ most and where the cost of a wrong choice is highest. Check them in a real trial, not from marketing pages.

scenario: Your two shortlisted tools both look good after a demo.
question: What is the best next step?

options.text: A two-week pilot with two tools: build real tables, one report and one automation, have three people use each, then score them with a weighted scorecard.
Choose the cheaper one and migrate everything at once.
Test all five available tools at the same time for a month.

why: Two tools keep effort focused. Real data and real users reveal problems a demo never will, and the decision should be written down with its reasoning and review date.

scenario: The team has decided on a tool. Someone asks about leaving it later.
question: What should you test in the pilot?

options.text: Export a table and open the file, check for stable unique IDs and list where else the data is referenced.
Nothing. Exit planning is pessimistic and can wait.
Assume the vendor will provide an export whenever you ask.

why: A tool you cannot leave has a hidden price. A short exit test costs an hour and may save weeks later.
